title: The Lost Colony of Roanoke: 115 People Vanished and Left One Word

beats.text: August eighteenth, fifteen ninety. An English sea captain steps onto a quiet beach on the Outer Banks, the narrow sandy islands of what is now North Carolina.
He is looking for his daughter and his baby granddaughter. Three years earlier, he left them here, together with more than a hundred other settlers.
His name is John White. He walks toward the settlement, and in the sand he sees fresh footprints. But the village he built is silent.
The houses have been taken down. Only a tall wall of tree trunks still stands around the empty ground. No one comes to meet him.
On a tree, someone has carved three letters: C, R, O. And on a post at the gate, in neat capital letters, is a whole word: CROATOAN.
There is no sign of a fight. There is no one at all. More than four hundred years later, we still do not know what happened to them.
This is the story of the Lost Colony of Roanoke. What do we truly know, what do we only guess, and what has simply been invented?
To understand the silence, we have to go back to fifteen eighty-four. England wants a foothold in North America, and Queen Elizabeth the First gives Walter Raleigh a charter to claim land.
There is a catch. If Raleigh has not planted a colony within seven years, he loses his rights to the land. So the clock is already ticking.
That summer, two English ships reach the Outer Banks. They return home with two local men named Manteo and Wanchese.
In fifteen eighty-five, Raleigh sends the first group of settlers: about one hundred and seven men, under a commander named Ralph Lane.
Almost at once, things go wrong. One of their ships hits a shoal and ruins most of the food. Relations with the local people soon turn hostile.
In the spring of fifteen eighty-six, Lane's men attack and kill the local leader, Pemisapan. Lane's men are exhausted and short of food.
In June, the fleet of Sir Francis Drake arrives. A violent storm hits, and Lane and his starving men decide to sail home with Drake.

Soon after, a second fleet arrives with supplies and finds the island deserted. It leaves fifteen men behind to hold the place. A year later, White finds no one, only some human bones. He believes they belonged to one of the fifteen.
Raleigh tries again, and this time the plan is different. The new settlers will be families, and they will found a town, called the City of Raleigh.
Their governor is John White, a gifted artist who painted the plants, animals and people of the New World. His watercolors survive today.
In the spring of fifteen eighty-seven, more than one hundred men, women and children sail from England. Most counts land near one hundred and fifteen.
In July they reach Roanoke Island. According to White, the fleet's pilot orders the sailors to leave the colonists there, and refuses to carry them any farther.
They find Lane's old fort taken apart and the houses overgrown with weeds. The colonists unload their supplies and begin to settle anyway.
Trouble comes quickly. One colonist, George Howe, is killed while hunting for crabs alone. Then the English strike a village they think is hostile.
It is a terrible mistake. They attack people from Croatoan, the home of their friend Manteo, instead of the enemies they were looking for.
On August eighteenth, fifteen eighty-seven, White's daughter Eleanor gives birth to a girl. She is named Virginia Dare, the first English child born in the Americas.
But supplies are running low, and winter is coming. The settlers beg their governor to sail back to England and bring help. White does not want to go.
Before he leaves, they make a plan. If the settlers must leave Roanoke, they will carve the name of their new home on a tree or a door post.
And if they are in danger, they will carve a cross above the name. That cross is the secret signal for trouble. Remember it.
They are already talking about moving about fifty miles inland, away from the coast. White leaves them to their plan.
He sails on August twenty-seventh. Behind him on the island are more than a hundred people, including his daughter and his granddaughter, only nine days old.
White reaches England in the autumn. But England is bracing for war. Spain is about to send a huge fleet of warships, the Armada, and the Queen forbids able ships to leave.
In the spring of fifteen eighty-eight, White manages to send two small ships. French raiders attack them, loot the supplies, and force them to turn back.
Then the war drags on. By fifteen eighty-nine, England's ships are busy fighting Spain, and no help is sent to Roanoke at all.
It takes White almost three years to get back to Roanoke. As far as we know, no help reaches the colonists in all that time.
At last, in the summer of fifteen ninety, White gets passage on two ships, the Hopewell and the Moonlight. On August twelfth, they anchor near Croatoan Island.
Three days later, the crews see a column of smoke rising from Roanoke Island. It is the first sign of anyone on the island.
On the seventeenth, a boat carrying Captain Spicer capsizes in the surf at the harbor entrance. Seven men drown.
That night, from the boats, the crews see the light of a great fire through the woods at the north end of the island.
At daybreak on the eighteenth, they land. The fire has burned only grass and rotten trees. In the sand, the men see the fresh footprints of local people.
They walk toward the old settlement. High on a tree along the way, they find three letters, carved with care: C, R, O.
White knows what it means. It is part of the plan they made. The colonists have gone to Croatoan, the place where Manteo was born.
Then they reach the entrance. The wall of tree trunks still stands, strong and tall. But the houses behind it have been taken down.
On one post, in clear capital letters, is the word CROATOAN. And White looks for the cross, the agreed signal of danger. There is none.
Nearby are five chests that the colonists had hidden. Three belonged to White himself. They have been dug up, and his belongings are scattered.
His books are torn from their covers. His maps and pictures are ruined by rain. His armor is almost eaten through by rust.
Still, there is no cross. White concludes that the colonists were not in danger. They had simply moved to Croatoan.
He wants to sail there at once. But a storm is building. A cable snaps, and the ship loses another anchor.
The ships are short of fresh water. The captains decide to head south, spend the winter in the Caribbean, and return to search in the spring.
They never do. Storms keep them from reaching Croatoan, and White sails home, arriving in England on October twenty-fourth. No Englishman is known to have seen those colonists again.
So what happened to them? Historians have three main ideas, and each one comes with evidence, and with problems.
The first idea: they went to Croatoan. The carving says so, and White believed it. Croatoan was an island about sixty miles south, home to friendly people.
In the early seventeen hundreds, a traveler named John Lawson visited the area. He wrote that some Hatteras people had gray eyes, and he suspected a link to the lost settlers.
In twenty-twenty, archaeologist Mark Horton reported European objects at a Native village on Hatteras Island, including part of a sword and a gun.
Some experts say this proves nothing about the colonists. Objects can travel through trade. So the Croatoan idea remains possible, but unproven.
The second idea: they moved inland, just as they had planned. In twenty twelve, researchers at the British Museum held one of White's own maps up to a light.
Under a paper patch, they found a hidden drawing of a small fort. It points to a place on the Albemarle Sound, inland from Roanoke Island.
Archaeologists call it Site X. There they found English pottery of a type used around the turn of the sixteen hundreds, and fragments of weapons.
The team suggests that a small group, perhaps six to ten colonists, may have lived there for a while. It would be a rare physical trace of them.
But the evidence is thin. The pottery could also come from the earlier colony, or from a trading post built decades later. Site X is a clue, not a conclusion.
The third idea comes from nature itself. In the nineteen-nineties, scientists studied the tree rings of centuries-old cypress trees along the coast.
The rings show that between fifteen eighty-seven and fifteen eighty-nine, the region suffered the worst three-year drought in eight hundred years.
A drought like that kills crops and dries up water. It would have hurt the settlers and the local people around them. The researchers call it a strong factor, not proof.
Over the centuries, other stories have grown around this mystery. Some are almost certainly false.
Early in the sixteen hundreds, a writer named William Strachey described a massacre of the colonists by a Native leader. Historians widely doubt his account.
Then there are the Dare Stones. Between nineteen thirty-seven and nineteen forty, dozens of stones turned up, carved with messages that claimed to come from the survivors.
In nineteen forty-one, a journalist exposed most of them as forgeries. The very first stone is still debated by experts today.
Some Lumbee people trace their ancestry to the Croatoan and the colonists. Historians say there is no firm proof, and DNA projects have not found a confirmed descendant.
Time has also erased evidence. Between eighteen fifty-one and nineteen seventy, the northern shore of Roanoke Island lost about nine hundred feet of land to erosion.
Whatever the colonists left there may now lie under water.
So let us separate fact from guess. It is certain that more than one hundred English settlers were left on Roanoke Island in fifteen eighty-seven.
It is certain that John White found the settlement empty three years later. It is certain that he found the word CROATOAN, and no cross.
And there is no confirmed sighting of those colonists after that. Everything else is a theory.
Perhaps they split up. Some may have gone south to Croatoan, others inland, and some may have died of hunger and drought. We simply do not know.
Mysteries like this are rarely solved by a single discovery. They are solved slowly, by small clues in the soil. Archaeologists are still digging today.
More than four hundred years later, a carved word on a post is still the only message the Lost Colony left behind.
What do you think it meant? Tell us in the comments, and come back tomorrow for another true mystery from history.
